strengths: The paper is clearly written and the core idea is simple and well-motivated: exploit the implicit token-level reward (log-ratio between the DPO-aligned model and its reference) that already exists after standard DPO training, requiring no extra training or auxiliary reward model.
The theoretical framing via the KL-regularized optimal policy (Eq. 6) is a clean way to explain why greedy decoding underuses the alignment signal learned by DPO.

The empirical evaluation is broad: 4 model scales across 2 model families, 6 preference datasets, comparisons against greedy SFT, greedy DPO, best-of-2, and EFT, plus a BoN-vs-AAD compute analysis, a beta-robustness study, a beam-search variant with entropy thresholding, and an iterative-DPO data-scarcity experiment.

The compute-matched comparison against BoN (Fig. 2) and the data-scaling experiment (Fig. 3) are informative, and the paper honestly reports limitations (two forward passes per token, requires access to the original SFT model) and provides a code link, training details, and full-finetuning ablations (Table 4).
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to existing inference-time alignment work. Maximizing a token-level log-ratio reward between an aligned and reference model is essentially the EFT/proxy-alignment/GenARM/DeRa idea (Mitchell et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024d), and the min-alpha filtering is directly borrowed from contrastive decoding (Li et al., 2023a) / min-p (Minh et al., 2025). The paper's differentiators (greedy argmax of the ratio rather than reweighting, filtering applied to pi_DPO) are incremental, and the related-work section does not clearly articulate why AAD is meaningfully distinct from decoding pi_SFT with EFT using the same model pair.

Circular evaluation risk: the headline metric (oracle reward R) is a Bradley-Terry reward model of exactly the type the DPO model was trained to maximize, and the win rates (W) appear to be computed by pairwise comparison with this same oracle. AAD maximizing the implicit reward may thus exploit the reward model family rather than genuinely improving alignment. There is no human evaluation, no diversity of evaluator types beyond AlpacaEval, and no analysis of whether outputs are degenerate or reward-hacked.

The AlpacaEval results (Table 2) are much weaker than the reward-model results (win rates ~0.65-0.82, sometimes below SFT), suggesting the large oracle-reward gains in Table 1 do not transfer to an external LLM-based evaluator; the paper does not discuss this discrepancy.

Statistical rigor is lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests anywhere; win rates are computed on a fixed prompt sample with no reporting of sample size, and results appear to be from single training runs.

The theoretical motivation is somewhat overstated: the observation that the KL-regularized optimal policy does not maximize reward pointwise is a restatement of the KL constraint (Eq. 2), and decoding to maximize reward arguably just moves along the KL-reward tradeoff rather than 'correcting inherited biases'. No theory is provided for why greedy maximization of the token-ratio (with min-alpha filtering) is a good approximation.

Several presentation defects: an incomplete sentence in Related Work ('These approaches typically' ends mid-sentence), typos ('againgst', 'traind', 'constrain', 'Agrilla' vs 'Argilla' inconsistency, '|piDPO' rendering, stray 's' after Fig. 11 caption), an over-interpreted qualitative analysis in Fig. 1, and the A.6 code link appears to be missing/truncated, weakening the reproducibility claim.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is underexplored for the proposed method itself: only alpha=0.1 (and alpha=0.7 in the beam study) is reported; no sensitivity analysis for alpha or the entropy threshold tau is given, and the beta values used across experiments are inconsistent (0.1 in training, 0.05 baseline in Fig. 4, 4 for EFT), making some comparisons hard to interpret.

strengths: The core idea is simple and well-motivated: exploiting the token-level log-ratio between the DPO-aligned model and its reference (an implicit token reward per Rafailov et al. 2024b) directly at decoding time, with min-α filtering to prevent degeneration.
The observation in Eq. (6) that even the KL-optimal policy π* can prefer lower-reward completions because it inherits biases of πSFT is a clean and correct motivating analysis.

The empirical evaluation is broad: 6 preference datasets, 4 model sizes across two families, an external-oracle protocol (Skywork/Starling RM) that avoids train-on-eval-prompt contamination, an AlpacaEval check, β-robustness analysis, BoN compute comparison, and full fine-tuning results in the appendix.
The iterative DPO experiment (Fig. 5) is a nice practical extension, showing that AAD-generated synthetic data nearly closes the gap to full-dataset training from only 10% of the preference data.
Compute-equivalence is explicitly considered (two forward passes for AAD vs. half-cost greedy and comparable-cost Bo2/EFT), and the code release is promised (Section A.6).
weaknesses: Limited originality. The proposed score ν = log(πDPO/πSFT) with token filtering is essentially a combination of contrastive decoding (Li et al., 2023a), min-p filtering (Minh et al., 2025), and EFT-style implicit token rewards (Mitchell et al., 2024). EFT already decodes by adding the reference-vs-aligned log-ratio as a token reward; AAD differs mainly in greedy argmax plus min-α filtering. The paper positions itself against EFT/GenARM/weak-to-strong search but never empirically compares to GenARM, DeRa, weak-to-strong search, ARGS, or DeAl, despite discussing them at length — the inference-time-alignment baseline set is too thin.

Evaluation validity concerns. All primary results (Table 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 5) are scored by an oracle reward model, and the win rates are model-based pairwise judgments. There is no human evaluation anywhere. Since AAD and DPO are both reward-maximizing procedures that can over-optimize the reward signal, consistently higher oracle reward does not unambiguously demonstrate better alignment; the AlpacaEval check (Table 2) uses only the default (GPT-4 style) evaluator and is presented only as win rates with no absolute quality measure. Confidence intervals or statistical significance are not reported for any comparison.

Some results undercut the headline claim. On AlpacaEval, AAD is only 'mostly' ahead (Table 2 shows AAD losing to several baselines, e.g., Nectar/Llama-3B/EFT region and Qwen settings), and in the full-finetuning appendix (Table 4) AAD falls below EFT on Skywork/Llama-1B (1.55 vs 2.00) and below Bo2/Greedy-DPO on HHRLHF/Llama-1B. The 'consistently outperforms' framing in the abstract is stronger than the evidence.

Inconsistent and under-justified hyperparameters. α = 0.1 is fixed for the main results but α = 0.7 is used for the beam-search study without explanation; β = 4 is used for the EFT baseline while DPO models use β = 0.1. There is no ablation over α, and no sensitivity analysis for the entropy threshold τ beyond one dataset.

The theoretical framing is thin. Eq. (6) is a two-line manipulation of Eq. (4); the paper claims AAD can be 'interpreted as implicit reward optimization' (abstract) but greedy token-wise maximization of a sequence-level log-ratio is not reward optimization in any formal sense, and no analysis connects greedy per-token argmax of ν to maximizing rDPO(x, y) (greedy argmax of a sum of per-token scores does not maximize the sum unless dominance conditions hold — this gap is never addressed).

Presentation is sloppy: 'againgst', 'This constrain ensures', 'Agrilla' vs 'Argilla' inconsistently, 'traind', 'helpfullness', a stray 's' ending the Fig. 11 caption, and the reproducibility URL in A.6 is truncated/absent. Figure 1's qualitative claims (e.g., that AAD alone 'directly addresses size') are anecdotal and not supported by quantitative evidence.

Limitations are mentioned only in a single conclusion sentence (two forward passes, need for the SFT/reference model). Notably, AAD requires access to the pre-DPO reference model, which weakens the claimed advantage over EFT-style methods (which can decode a third unaligned model) and over explicit-reward methods in proprietary-weight settings — a comparison the paper's motivation implicitly rests on but never confronts.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained: decoding the DPO-aligned model by greedily maximizing the token-level log-likelihood ratio with the SFT reference model (plus min-α plausibility filtering), turning the implicit DPO reward into a decoding objective without extra training or auxiliary models.

The motivating observation (the KL-constrained optimum can rank completions inconsistently with the true reward, Eq. 6) is correct and connects the method to the DPO-as-Q-function view of Rafailov et al. (2024b), giving the heuristic a reasonable theoretical grounding.

The empirical study is broad and fairly compute-fair: 4 models across 2 families (0.6B–8B), 6 preference datasets, LoRA and full fine-tuning variants (Table 4), win rate + oracle reward metrics, BoN comparisons up to N=50, a β-robustness ablation (Fig. 4), a data-scaling study (Fig. 3), and a genuinely interesting iterative-DPO experiment showing AAD-generated data nearly closes the gap to full-data training with only 10% of preference data (Fig. 5).

The paper is transparent about practical failure modes of naive reward-ratio decoding (degenerate completions, numerical instability from small reference probabilities) and addresses them explicitly with min-α filtering, plus a beam-search entropy-thresholding fix; limitations (two forward passes per token, need for the SFT reference) are honestly stated.
External evaluation on AlpacaEval and off-the-shelf oracles (Skywork, Starling) for two datasets partially mitigates the circularity of evaluating with self-trained reward models.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. The method is essentially contrastive decoding (Li et al., 2023a) applied to the DPO/SFT pair, which is very close to EFT (Mitchell et al., 2024), GenARM (Xu et al., 2025), weak-to-strong search (Zhou et al., 2024), and DeRa (Liu et al., 2024d), all of which use the same reference–aligned log-ratio signal at decoding time; the main deltas are the greedy (non-search) formulation and min-p-style filtering. The paper cites these works but does not clearly delineate its technical distinction or compare against the closest competitors (e.g., weak-to-strong search, DeAl, ARGS).

Circularity/over-optimization risk in the headline results. The primary metric is reward from Bradley–Terry oracles trained on the same preference distributions used for DPO, while AAD directly maximizes the implicit reward; high oracle reward could partly reflect reward-model exploitation rather than genuine alignment. The external AlpacaEval results (Table 2) show much smaller margins than Table 1, and the LLM-judge methodology (which evaluator version, length bias, number of sampled comparisons, CIs) is under-reported. No human evaluation is provided.

No statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests anywhere; the number of evaluation prompts is not stated. Given many cells are close (e.g., Qwen 0.6B on Skywork, several HHRLHF results), it is hard to judge whether 'consistently outperforms' holds everywhere.

The theoretical framing slightly overstates: greedy per-token maximization of ν does not provably maximize the sequence-level implicit reward, and the practical method is a heuristic (argmax of a log-ratio over a min-α-filtered candidate set) whose connection to Eq. 8's 'maximize r_DPO' is only approximate; the α and (for beam search) τ hyperparameters are essentially hand-tuned heuristics with limited ablation (α=0.1 for generation vs α=0.7 in the beam experiment; β ablation on only one dataset).

Presentation has numerous errors that should have been caught: inconsistent dataset naming ('Agrilla' vs 'Argilla'), typos ('againgst', 'This constrain ensures', 'traind', 'maximize' missing the β log), a garbled reward definition (r_DPO(x,y) = β π_DPO/π_SFT without the log in Section 4), a malformed Eq. 5, a truncated sentence at the end of the related-work section ('These approaches typically'), and 'us' at the end of a Figure 11 caption. Figure 1's qualitative claims read as post-hoc rationalization of a single cherry-picked example.

The synthetic-data claim in the abstract ('produce high-quality synthetic data to improve alignment under standard decoding') is only demonstrated with AAD-generated chosen responses paired with nucleus-sampled rejected responses — i.e., the data pipeline depends on AAD for positives, and the iterative DPO experiment is confined to one model/dataset; a comparison with self-generated-data baselines (e.g., Bo2 or EFT-generated pairs) is missing to establish that AAD specifically is responsible for the gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link promised in Section A.6 appears to be a placeholder, and key details (evaluation set sizes, prompt sampling procedure, number of win-rate comparisons, judge configuration) are absent.

strengths: The method is simple, training-free, and well-motivated: AAD exploits the SFT-vs-DPO log-likelihood ratio as a token-level advantage with min-α filtering, and the appendix provides a coherent theoretical derivation (building on Rafailov et al., 2024b's Q-function view) that justifies the token-level score.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad and compute-controlled: 6 preference datasets, 4 model scales across two families, open-source OLMo-2 DPO checkpoints, comparisons against BoN up to N=50 (Figure 2), beam search (Figures 7-8), contrastive decoding with external 'amateur' models (Table 3), and full fine-tuning (Table 8) all support the central claim.

The paper honestly discusses limitations: two forward passes per token, the need for SFT access, the restriction to the SFT+DPO pipeline, and mixed results when combined with PPO (Table 10). The β-robustness analysis (Figure 5) and data-scaling results (Figure 4, Table 7) add useful practical insight.

The iterative DPO application (Figure 6, Table 9) is a practical contribution, showing that AAD-generated synthetic data nearly closes the gap to full-dataset training using only 10% of preference data, with replication on additional datasets.
weaknesses: Limited originality relative to prior work. Greedy/log-ratio decoding of a model using a reference-aligned pair is essentially the mechanism of emulated fine-tuning (Mitchell et al., 2024), proxy tuning (Liu et al., 2024a), GenARM, DeRa, and weak-to-strong decoding, and AAD's min-α restriction is directly borrowed from contrastive decoding. The paper does not precisely articulate what is new beyond applying the log-ratio to the DPO model itself; the relationship between AAD and the EFT baseline (and why the EFT variant is configured with πSFT for both base and reference) is underspecified, raising the concern that a properly configured EFT baseline might be much closer to AAD than reported.

Potential evaluation circularity. The primary metric is an oracle reward model trained on the same preference data used to train the DPO model, and AAD explicitly maximizes an implicit version of that reward; large reward-model gains may partially reflect reward-model over-optimization. The external-judge evidence is notably weaker: under the GPT-4 AlpacaEval evaluator (Table 2) several cells are near or below 0.6-0.65, and human evaluation (Table 5) shows only 58.7% preference over greedy DPO on a single dataset/model. The paper does not adequately reconcile these discrepancies with the large reward-model margins.

Reproducibility is undermined by missing artifacts: the 'Code available at' statement on page 1 and the code URL in Section A.5 are both blank. Combined with unreported confidence intervals / prompt counts for the main Table 1 and the ambiguous caption of Table 2 (win rates are not clearly attributed to methods), this makes independent verification harder than it should be.

Some experimental choices are not well justified, e.g., a single α = 0.1 is claimed to transfer across all settings but only ablated on a 3B model with three datasets (Figure 3); the human evaluation covers only one dataset-model pair; and Bo2 with a separately trained picker reward model is arguably a weaker compute-matched baseline than BoN with the same picker at the dashed-line compute point in Figure 2.

Presentation issues: Figure 1 and the qualitative examples (Figures 11-14) are given disproportionate weight in the narrative relative to the quantitative evidence, and several tables/figures (Table 2 caption, Figure 5 axes) require careful decoding by the reader.

strengths: The paper is well written and clearly organized, with a clean derivation (Appendix A.1) motivating the token-level log-ratio score via the token-MDP view of DPO from Rafailov et al. (2024b).

The empirical evaluation is broad: 6 preference datasets, 4 model families across two scales, plus OLMo-2 open-source checkpoints, full fine-tuning ablations, data-scaling and beta-robustness studies, beam-search and contrastive-decoding comparisons, iterative DPO experiments, and a human study.
The method is simple and practical, requiring only the DPO model and its SFT reference, with a single hyperparameter (alpha) that reportedly transfers across datasets and scales without tuning.

The paper is reasonably honest about limitations: it restricts its main claim to the SFT+DPO pipeline, reports the mixed PPO results (Table 10), discusses the two-forward-pass overhead, and includes latency/throughput benchmarks.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core method is essentially contrastive decoding (Li et al., 2023b) where the 'amateur' model is the DPO model's own SFT reference, which is precisely the DPO implicit reward r_DPO = beta * log(pi_DPO/pi_SFT). The paper itself shows (Table 3) that generic CD with Instruct models underperforms, but the conceptual step from 'use SFT as the contrast model' is small, and closely related inference-time methods (EFT/GenARM, weak-to-strong decoding, DeRa) are cited rather than empirically compared head-to-head.

The primary evaluation relies on oracle reward models trained by the authors on the same preference distribution used to train the aligned model. A method that explicitly maximizes a token-level reward-like signal at decoding time is naturally susceptible to over-optimizing such an evaluator, i.e., the reported rewards may partly reflect Goodharting the metric rather than genuine alignment gains.

The evidence that is harder to game is weaker: the human study covers only 502 judgments from a single 3B model on one dataset, and the headline win rate against greedy DPO is only 58.7% — a modest margin compared to the large oracle-reward gaps in Table 1. This discrepancy is not analyzed in depth.
Missing comparisons to the most similar inference-time alignment baselines (e.g., GenARM, weak-to-strong search, ARGS/DeAl), which weakens the claim of 'consistently outperforms strong baselines'.

Several presentation issues undermine confidence: the qualitative Figure 1 reads as a cherry-picked example with debatable claims (e.g., that AAD alone 'addresses size' of a dog breed); Table 2 and Table 4 omit AAD's own AlpacaEval entries and leave ambiguous what baselines' win rates are measured against; the 'Code available at' footnote and Appendix A.5 reproducibility section are empty, which is a reproducibility concern for a methods paper.

The theoretical framing is largely a restatement of known results (KL-regularized MDP solution, Q-function view of DPO); the argument in Section 4 that the optimal KL-constrained policy can rank a higher-reward completion below a lower-reward one is straightforward and does not by itself justify greedy per-token maximization, whose behavior is instead handled heuristically via min-alpha filtering borrowed from contrastive decoding.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation: six preference datasets, four model scales across two families (Llama, Qwen), plus open-source OLMo-2-7B/13B DPO checkpoints, covering both LoRA and full fine-tuning regimes.

Evaluation goes beyond reward-model circularity: external off-the-shelf oracles for Skywork/Nectar (not trained on evaluation prompts), an AlpacaEval GPT-4 judge, and a human study with 40 raters and 502 pairwise judgments, all of which corroborate the reward-model results.

Clear theoretical motivation building on Rafailov et al. (2024b), deriving the token-level log-ratio as an approximate advantage (Appendix A.1), and an honest analysis of why unconstrained maximization degenerates and how min-α filtering addresses it.

Thorough ablations: effect of α (Figure 3), DPO β robustness (Figure 5), data-scaling regimes (Figure 4, Table 7), beam search stabilization via entropy thresholding (Figure 7), throughput benchmarking, and epoch effects.

Genuinely useful extension showing AAD-generated data enables iterative DPO that nearly closes the gap to full-dataset training from only 10% of the preference data, with replication on additional datasets (Table 9).
Limitations are candidly discussed: two forward passes per token, restriction to the SFT+DPO pipeline, and mixed results when combined with PPO-trained models (Table 10).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core mechanism (argmax over log πDPO/πSFT restricted to plausible tokens) is essentially contrastive decoding with the SFT model as the 'amateur', and decoding-time reweighting of DPO models via the reference log-ratio is already explored by DeRa (Liu et al., 2024d) and EFT-style approaches. The paper's own related-work section acknowledges the closeness, but the mechanistic delta over these baselines is modest.

The headline claim of 'consistently outperforms' is overstated. In the full fine-tuning appendix (Table 8), AAD loses to EFT on several settings (e.g., HHRLHF 1B: 0.26 vs -0.06; Skywork 1B: 2.00 vs 1.55), and gains on Qwen 0.6B are much smaller than for larger models. AlpacaEval win rates (Table 2) are moderate (0.73–0.82).
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the win rates in the main results (Table 1), despite many of the margins being modest.

The theoretical justification is informal: Equation (18) holds for the optimal π*, but the argument that the DPO-trained log-ratio is a reliable token-level advantage for arbitrary (and particularly low-probability) tokens is asserted rather than characterized; the paper handles this empirically via α-filtering rather than theoretically.

The main results rely on oracle reward models trained on the same distribution as the aligned models, which invites reward-model exploitation; the external-oracle and AlpacaEval mitigations only cover two of the six datasets.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the code URL is left blank ('Code available at'), and although training hyperparameters are detailed, the missing artifact weakens the reproducibility claim.

Compute-equivalence framing is somewhat favorable: Bo2 and EFT are claimed comparable in cost, but Bo2's parallel generation and AAD's two sequential forward passes are not strictly equivalent, and the throughput analysis (0.5–0.75× greedy) shows a real overhead that is underemphasized in the main text.
